background: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt . The group subsequently published data allegedly obtained from the company, which included 373k unique email addresses across records relating to users, sales leads and CyrusOne employees. The data largely consisted of corporate contact information, including names, physical addresses, phone numbers and job titles.
It also included support tickets and other information related to the organisation's operations.
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
motive: In August 2026, data centre operator CyrusOne was the target of a ShinyHunters "pay or leak" extortion attempt .
outcome: 373,460 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Email addresses, Employers, Job titles, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses, Support tickets.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Employers
fields.why: Connects a personal account to a workplace, which is how attackers pivot from a person to a company.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Job titles
fields.why: Identifies who has access to what, which is how targets for business email compromise are picked.

fields.name: Support tickets
fields.why: Adds detail to a profile that can be assembled from several breaches at once.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
